title: Ang 660–662: Dhanasri begins
tomorrow: what if the whole night sky were a plate of lamps?

lines: FIVE A.M. ON A BIG DAY.
THE FEAR HAS NOWHERE TO GO.
TO WHOM SHOULD I CRY OUT?
cards: Five in the morning on a big day: an interview, a surgery, a flight, a wedding. The house is dark, the phone is bright, and the fear has nowhere to go. Who do you tell at that hour?
That's yesterday's question. On ang 660, Guru Nanak opens raga Dhanasri with exactly that hour. My soul is afraid, he sings.
To whom should I cry out?

teach.b: The opening, in paraphrase: My soul is afraid; to whom should I cry out?

teach.h: THE ONE WHO MAKES PAIN FORGOTTEN.
teach.b: I serve the one who makes pain forgotten, the Giver, forever and ever.
And the line that comes back like a refrain: my Master is always new, always giving. Notice the order. The fear comes first, and nobody scolds it.

A new raga, a first hymn, and its first line is fear. Then comes the question, and the question is the turn: not whether to be afraid, but who to bring it to. The answer isn't a technique for calming down.
It's a person to turn toward, the one who makes pain forgotten. And that one is called always new: not worn out by the last time you came scared, or the time before that.
So what does Dhanasri give you this week, for the five a.m. fear?

teach.h: SAY IT, AND TAKE IT SOMEWHERE.
teach.b: Permission to say it plainly, and somewhere to take it.
So the raga Dhanasri doesn't open on praise or a rule. Its first hymn opens on a scared soul asking where to go.

how: Sikhs read Guru Nanak's opening Dhanasri hymn, 'jeeo darat hai aapna', in the Guru Granth Sahib; it is sung in kirtan, its refrain naming the Master who is always new and always giving.

where Guru Nanak opens the raga Dhanasri

games.q: Dhanasri's first hymn — tap the pairs.
p: to whom should I cry out?

s: Guru Nanak's first Dhanasri hymn says the faithful don't feel fear
it opens with fear: my soul is afraid; to whom should I cry out?
the hymn calls the Master always new
my Master is always new, always giving, forever.
the hymn's answer to fear is a breathing technique
the answer is someone to turn to: the one who makes pain forgotten.

games.q: it's the morning of your big exam and you can't stop shaking. a friend texts 'you good?' what fits Dhanasri's first hymn?
o: say it plainly: 'scared, honestly,' and turn toward someone who helps.
say 'all good!' because admitting fear means you've lost your faith.
don't answer; fear is private and shouldn't be shared with anyone.
games.why: Guru Nanak's hymn says the fear first, then asks who to bring it to. the turn is toward the Giver who makes pain forgotten.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write the fear you're carrying this week in a few plain words, with nothing to soften it. Then set the pen down, put your hand flat over the words, and sit.
If you pray, you can bring it to the one Guru Nanak calls the Giver; if not, simply let it be said.

wordCard.voice: Ang 660. Where raga Dhanasri begins: Guru Nanak's scared soul, asking whom to cry out to, and turning to the Giver who is always new.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Dhanasri, the raga that begins on ang 660 with Guru Nanak's scared soul.

carryVoice: Keep this: Dhanasri, the raga that lets the fear be said first, even on a wedding morning. Go gently.
